Subnanometer metal cluster catalysts have garnered signiﬁcant attention due
to their multi-site synergistic catalytic capabilities. However, constrained by
classical sintering theory, metal clusters are prone to sintering and growth,
which makes it challenging for them to stably exist at high temperatures.
Prevailing strategies predominantly focus on the synthesis pathways from
atoms to clusters, while overlooking the bidirectional regulation potential of
metal particle dynamic reconstruction. This study transcends conventional
paradigms by proposing a reverse regulation strategy from particles to clus-
ters. The disadvantage of high temperature is strategically converted into
driving forces for particle dispersion through the rational design of catalytic
environments and metal-support interactions. Through a comprehensive
combination of in situ characterization techniques and theoretical calcula-
tions, the interfacial atomic migration pathways and energy evolution during
dynamic dispersion are systematically investigated. Furthermore, the forma-
tion process and underlying mechanism of stable Ni clusters are elucidated.
The optimized 10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst exhibits a remarkably high H2 pro-
duction rate (500 °C, 279.2 mmolH2·gNi
−1·min−1) and exceptional thermal sta-
bility. This work not only provides a methodology for developing thermally
stable cluster catalysts but also fundamentally reveals the mechanism of
reverse sintering from the perspective of atomic migration kinetics and ther-
modynamic steady-state reconstruction.

through the construction of strong coordination or rigid conﬁnement
environments9,10. While this passive defense strategy can stabilize
clusters under mild conditions8, it fails to fundamentally overcome
energy barriers. Consequently, under high-temperature conditions,
such clusters inevitably aggregate into larger metal particles11. Notably,
high-temperature conditions can also generate abundant reactive
oxygen species on the surface of oxide support through the enhanced
lattice oxygen migration efﬁciency and surface atomic migration
efﬁciency12,13. Such highly reactive surfaces of oxide support can
strongly interact with the metal phase14, which may enable reverse
transformation from particles to clusters. However, current studies on
metal particle dispersion are largely conﬁned to speciﬁc supports such
as Mo2N15,16. The systematic investigations into the reverse dispersion
kinetics of metal particles and the migration pathways of interfacial
atomic remains insufﬁcient, which directly hinders the rational design
of stable cluster catalysts for high-temperature applications.
Utilizing speciﬁc catalytic reaction conditions to in situ modulate
metal-support interaction (MSI) represents a feasible strategy for
achieving the transformation from particles to clusters. As an effective
method for generating high-purity COx-free hydrogen, the ammonia
decomposition reaction requires a high temperature (> 550 °C) to
achieve complete conversion17,18, which precisely facilitates efﬁcient
oxygen migration. The strongly reducing atmosphere can also induce
the enrichment of oxygen vacancies in reducible oxide supports19.
Thus, ammonia decomposition is an ideal reaction for investigating
the reverse dispersion of particles. Furthermore, the selection of
supports with highly reactive surfaces and excellent tunability is con-
ducive to constructing a strong MSI that surpasses the inherent lattice
forces of metal particles20. The exceptional oxygen storage capacity,
along with the ability to modulate interactions with active metals by
tuning the concentration of oxygen vacancies, renders CeO2 a pre-
ferred material21,22. However, the morphology and structure of CeO2
are susceptible to sintering and collapse at high temperatures, which
reduces oxygen migration capacity and compromises the anchoring
function23. Studies have demonstrated that the incorporation of La can
induce lattice distortion in CeO2 support, and consequently enhance
its high-temperature stability through the generated surface stress24.
Additionally, electron transfer between the metal and the support can
further enhance the interaction25. The catalytic environment and the
strong MSI effect collectively create conditions for reverse regulation
from particles to clusters. Analyzing the atomic-scale reconstruction
mechanism and energy evolution law in this dynamic dispersion pro-
cess is not only expected to establish an effective strategy for con-
structing high-temperature stable clusters, but also instrumental in
advancing the transition of heterogeneous catalysis from static active
site construction to dynamic adaptive regulation.
Herein, Ni-based catalysts supported on La-doped CeO2 (10Ni/
30La-CeO2, where nLa: nCe = 3: 7) and undoped CeO2 (10Ni/CeO2)
were synthesized respectively to catalyze the ammonia decomposition
reaction. By means of high-angle annular dark-ﬁeld scanning trans-
mission electronmicroscopy (HAADF-STEM)and in situ environmental
transmission electron microscopy (ETEM), the structural evolution
process of Ni particles transforming into Ni clusters in situ under a
high-temperature and reducing atmosphere was clearly elucidated.
Combining experimental investigations with theoretical calculations,
it was indicated that the in situ formation of stable Ni clusters can be
attributed to multiple factors. The surface stress engendered by La
doping effectively prevented the collapse of the CeO2 structure at high
temperatures. Subsequently, the further enhanced MSI effect and
efﬁcient oxygen migration enabled the retention of a greater number
of reactive O species on the surface of the support. Ultimately, the
formation of strong Ni-O-La and Ni-O-Ce bonding interactions induced
the dispersion of Ni particles to achieve a thermodynamic steady state.
The successful construction of a stable Ni cluster catalyst has enabled a
H2 production rate (500 °C, 279.2 mmolH2·gNi
−1·min−1) and exceptional
thermal stability. The reverse regulation strategy of inducing particle
redispersion successfully transforms the disadvantage of high tem-
perature into a driving force for the transition from particles to clus-
ters. Undoubtedly, this work offers an innovative solution to
overcoming the long-standing challenge of high-temperature sintering
in catalysts and provides novel insights for the development of high-
temperature stable cluster catalysts.

ods doped with La were prepared via the hydrothermal method. TEM
images showed that both CeO2 and 30La-CeO2 exhibited regular
nanorod morphologies, with La doping exerting minimal impact on
the structural characteristics (Supplementary Fig. 1). Then, Ni was

ges of the catalyst, a series of pretreatments were performed. The
catalyst, subjected to 12 h of gradient heating treatment with NH3 (for
the speciﬁc treatment procedure, see Supplementary Fig. 1), was
designated as the used catalyst. No signiﬁcant aggregation was
observed in the used 10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 2),
which suggested that it possessed favorable thermal stability.
The structural characteristics of the catalyst and the state trans-
formations of Ni species under various pretreatment conditions were
systematically analyzed by high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and HAADF-
STEM. The lattice fringe of the rod-like support was 0.31 nm, which
indicated that La doping did not alter the crystal structure of the CeO2
matrix. The corresponding energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) mapping
conﬁrmed localized Ni enrichment (Supplementary Fig. 3). No lattice
fringes corresponding to La species were observed in the 10Ni/30La-
CeO2 catalyst, indicating their high dispersion. It was noteworthy that
the Ni species on the surface of the 10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst under-
went signiﬁcant changes at different treatment stages. Firstly, HAADF-
STEM analysis revealed a large number of particles with sizes of
5−10 nm on the surface of the 10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst (Fig. 1a), which
was treated with NH3 at 500 °C for 0.5 h. Further, only a limited
number of Ni particles along with a substantial amount of Ni clusters
were observed after being treated at 600 °C for 1 h (Fig. 1b, Supple-
mentary Fig. 4). On this basis, the dispersion of Ni species was mark-
edly improved when the treatment time was extended to 120 h. The
metallic Ni particles were no longer detectable on the surface of the
10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst. A signiﬁcant number of stable Ni clusters
were observed, with an average size of 1−2 nm (Fig. 1c, Supplementary
Fig. 5). The EDX results (Supplementary Fig. 6), combined with ADF
intensity line-proﬁle analysis (Supplementary Fig. 7) obtained from the
30La-CeO2 nanorod edge regions, conﬁrmed the presence of Ni clus-
ters on the surface. In contrast, after being subjected to the same
treatments, the structure of the 10Ni/CeO2 catalyst collapsed, and a
large number of metallic Ni particles with sizes of 5−10 nm precipitated
(Supplementary Fig. 8 and 9). The identiﬁcation of three distinct states
of Ni species, captured through the prolonged treatment time, marked
the beginning of in-depth research into reverse dispersion from par-
ticles to clusters.
In situ dispersion process of Ni particles. In order to directly
observe the formation process of these Ni clusters, in situ aberration-
corrected ETEM was employed to characterize the 10Ni/30La-CeO2
catalyst26. The nanoparticles gradually contracted when the tempera-
ture increased from room temperature to 450 °C under a H2 atmo-
sphere (Fig. 2a, b). Then, the particles completely dispersed upon
further increasing the temperature to 600 °C, and the highly dispersed
state was retained even after returning to ambient temperature
(Fig. 2c, d). Additional in situ ETEM images collected from multiple
distinct regions under identical treatment conditions exhibited the
same evolution trend of particles to clusters (Supplementary Fig. 10).

In addition, to elucidate the phase transition and dispersion beha-
vior of Ni species, in situ STEM experiments were conducted under
continuous heating conditions at 450 °C and 600 °C, respectively. The
10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst initially underwent reduction at 450 °C (Fig. 2e,
Supplementary Fig. 13), with NiO transforming into metallic Ni, as evi-
denced by crystal structure analysis (Fig. 2g, h). Upon further heating,
both NiO and Ni nanoparticles progressively dispersed, ultimately
forming fully dispersed Ni clusters at 600 °C (Fig. 2f). Nevertheless, no
dispersion of Ni particles was observed on the surface of the 10Ni/CeO2
catalyst at 600 °C (Supplementary Fig. 14). This distinct contrast pow-
erfully underscores that extended treatment time and elevated tem-
perature alone are not the primary drivers of dispersion. Instead, it is La
doping that enables this phenomenon, a conclusion further corrobo-
rated by subsequent structural characterizations.
Structural determination of the 10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst. X-ray
diffraction (XRD) was employed to investigate the structure of La-
doped CeO2. The analysis revealed only the characteristic diffraction
peaks of CeO2, which exhibited a notable downshift (0.54°) upon La
doping, indicating the lattice expansion (Fig. 3a). The downshift in the
diffraction peak, together with the uniform elemental distribution and
the absence of any diffraction peaks or lattice fringes corresponding to
other La species, collectively conﬁrmed the complete incorporation of
La3+ into the CeO2 lattice. Fourier Transform infrared spectroscopy
(FTIR) was utilized to further validate the existence form of the Ni
species. Three distinct CO adsorption bands were observed on the
10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst surface (Fig. 3b). The peaks at 2170 cm−1 and
2165 cm−1 were assigned to CO adsorbed on Ce3+ ions27. The red peaks
corresponded to CO bound to Niδ+ species28, while the blue peaks were
characteristic of CO adsorbed on metallic Ni0. Quantitative analysis
revealed that the 10Ni/30La-CeO2 catalyst exhibited a signiﬁcantly
higher proportion of Niδ+ species (51.1%) compared to the 10Ni/CeO2
reference (30.6%), demonstrating the promotional effect of La doping
on the stabilization of oxidized Ni sites. The electronic states of Ni
species were further investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectro-
scopy (XPS). While only Ni2+ species were detected in all the as-

10Ni/30La-CeO2 (43%) was notably higher than that in 10Ni/CeO2 (31%),
indicating a signiﬁcantly greater concentration of OVs. The formation
of abundant OVs and the increase in Ce3+ also conversely corroborated
the successful doping of La. The role of increased OVs during the
ammonia decomposition reaction was investigated through in situ
Raman spectroscopy with H2 and NH3 switching. The Raman peaks at
417 cm−1 and 588 cm−1 corresponded to the symmetric vibration mode

ﬂuorite cubic structure, respectively. The relative strength ratio of

centration within the catalyst. Upon switching the test atmosphere

plementary Fig. 31). Notably, 10Ni/30La-CeO2 demonstrated superior

To further understand the mechanism of ammonia decomposi-
tion, DFT calculations were performed. The enhanced electrophilicity
and alkalinity of the La-doped catalyst signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced the
adsorption and activation of NH3. The calculated NH3 adsorption
energy was ‒0.57 eV on Ni3O/CeO2−x (111) and ‒0.66 eV on Ni3O/
LaCeO2−x (111), indicating stronger NH3 binding strength on the La-
doped surface (Supplementary Fig. 33–35). Moreover, the activation
barriers for N–H bond cleavage at the Ni-slab interface were sig-
niﬁcantly reduced in the La-doped system. Speciﬁcally, the barriers for
the three N–H scissions were 1.17, 1.20, and 0.81 eV on Ni3O/
LaCeO2−x(111), compared to 1.54, 1.30, and 0.65 eV on the undoped
Ni3O/CeO2−x(111). These results conﬁrmed that La doping lowered the
activation energy barrier for the elementary step of N–H bond clea-
vage, thus promoting more efﬁcient NH3 decomposition, which was
corroborated by NH3/D2-TPSR (Supplementary Fig. 36). Steady-state
turnover frequencies (TOFs), obtained from the calculated steady-
state surface coverages, also showed that the onset temperature for
